title: The Age of Dinosaurs, Beginning to End
description: Tonight, the entire age of the dinosaurs, from the beginning of it to the end of it, in order, without hurrying. About a hundred and sixty-five million years, at a pace meant for falling asleep.

There is an asteroid in this story and you already know about it. It arrives near the end, it gets a short chapter — shorter than the chapter about ferns — and it is not the ending. The ending is the chapter after it, and that one is about birds.
No jeopardy, no countdown, nothing waiting in the dark. Everything here finished a very long time ago, and most of it did not finish at all.
Best with the lights off.

title: The First Forests on Earth
description: Tonight, the first forests. Roughly three hundred and eighty-five million years ago, on a coastline in what is now New York State, plants worked out how to stand up.

Nothing happens in this story. There is nothing to brace for. It is about trees learning to be tall, which took about twenty-five million years, had no day on which it happened, and made no noise at all. The tallest living thing on land at the time was not a plant, and nobody is sure what it was.
You do not need to follow closely or remember any of the names. If you drift off in the middle and wake up at the end with no idea how you got there, that is the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: Sauropods, the Largest Animals on Land
description: Tonight, the largest animals that have ever walked on land, taken slowly and in no particular hurry. About a hundred and forty million years of them, at a pace meant for falling asleep.

Nothing happens in this one. Nothing hunts anything. There are animals in this episode that could have eaten the animals in this episode, and they are not invited, because the moment a predator appears you start waiting for something.
It is not a story that runs from a beginning to an end. It is a hundred quiet facts, gathered into groups, told in order, and the number is never counted out loud.

An egg the size of a grapefruit, from an animal the length of a tennis court. A neck bone taller than your table is long. Two of the largest creatures ever found, both of which have gone missing. And, at the end, a hole in a riverbed in Texas that you can put your own foot inside.
Best with the lights off.

title: The Western Interior Seaway, the Inland Sea That Split America in Two
description: Tonight, a sea that doesn't exist anymore, in a place where there is no sea at all. Kansas. Nebraska. For about thirty-four million years, a warm, shallow ocean ran straight through the middle of North America, from the Arctic Ocean to the Gulf of Mexico, and split the continent in two.

Nothing hunts anything in this one. There are two entirely unrelated kinds of large animal beneath the surface, a coiled shell and a straight one drifting through open water, and something gliding low over it at night, and none of them are in any danger, because the moment a predator appears you start waiting for something.

It is not a chase and it is not a countdown. It's a sea arriving from two directions and meeting in the middle, a floor built by a snowfall that never stopped for five million years, and then, slowly, over twenty million more, a sea leaving the same way it came, until there was nothing left of it but the shape of the ground.
You do not need to follow closely. If you drift off before it's over and wake up with no idea how you got there, that is the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: The Coal Forests, When Insects Grew as Big as Gulls
description: Tonight, a world breathing air richer than the air in the room you're lying in right now. For about sixty million years, huge tracts of the land near the equator stood as forest — dense, strange, built nothing like a modern one — and huge tracts of that forest were, one way or another, on their way to becoming something else entirely.

There are some very large animals in this one. An insect with a gull's wingspan. A millipede longer than you are tall. Neither is anything to be wary of. The insect eats other insects, calmly, the way insects always have. The millipede almost certainly ate old leaves. Nothing tonight hunts, or is hunted, or is described that way, however large it gets.

It's a story about an atmosphere thick enough to grow giants, a forest that photosynthesised through its bark, and a small, dry-skinned animal that quietly worked out how to leave water behind for good — found inside the hollow stump of one of this episode's own trees. Underneath it all, a swamp turning slowly into the single largest fuel reserve this planet has ever laid down, one drowned forest at a time.
You do not need to follow closely. If you drift off before the forest does, and wake up with no idea how you got there, that is the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: What Came After the Asteroid, How Earth Recovered in 10 Million Years
description: Tonight, a world that has just lost three out of every four species it had only a few days before, waking up in the ash and starting, almost immediately, to grow back. Nothing tonight happens at the moment of the asteroid — that story already happened, on an earlier evening — this one begins in the quiet afterward, and stays there for the next ten million years.

It's a story about ferns pushing up through burned ground before almost anything else does, a bird finding somewhere to nest again after nearly every one of its cousins didn't make it through, and a mammal the size of a mouse growing, within about a million years, into something the size of a large dog. Nothing tonight is in danger. Everything you hear about is already living on the far side of the worst of it.

Some of this is unusually well documented — the fern spike sits in the very same layer of rock, worldwide, as the iridium that first gave this event away. Other parts are genuinely still argued about by the people who study them: exactly how narrow the surviving line of birds was, and exactly how long a forest or an ocean needs before it counts as properly recovered. The episode says so, rather than picking the tidy answer.
You do not need to follow closely. If you're asleep before the forests are grown back, that's the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: The Cambrian Explosion, When the First Eyes Arrived
description: Tonight goes back further than this collection ever has — past the dinosaurs, past the coal forests, to a stretch of ocean more than half a billion years old, when almost nothing alive could tell one shape from another at any distance. In a little over fifty million years, that changes completely: shells appear almost everywhere within a short window of time, an eye arrives good enough to actually see with, and an ocean that had spent three billion years mostly sitting still becomes a world of animals noticing one another for the first time.

This one touches something the channel hasn't had to touch this directly before — real predators, real defences. It's told entirely through the noticing and the answering: a shell thickening, a body curling shut, a burrow going a little deeper. Nothing here describes the moment anything actually gets caught.

Some of tonight rests on work only a year or two old, including a genuine correction to one of the most famous animals in this whole story — its classic "armoured hunter" reputation doesn't survive contact with current evidence. Other parts are honestly, actively disputed right now: what actually set this whole event in motion is one of the oldest open questions in evolutionary biology, and nobody studying it today claims to have closed it.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the shells finish arriving, that's the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: The First Animals on Land, as Told by Their Footprints
description: Tonight is about the first steps out of the sea — and the first thing to take them, as far as anyone can currently tell, was not a fish. Over roughly a hundred million years, from a bare shore to one with forests behind it, small many-legged animals were coming and going at the water's edge long before anything with a backbone.

It is told through those tracks: rows of tiny dents in ancient sand, a small millipede in Scotland whose breathing pores say it breathed air, a lung that turns out to be older than the land, and a fin that became a limb underwater. Not one heroic crossing, but many, most of which left almost nothing behind.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. Two research teams still disagree by about fourteen million years on how old that millipede is. The famous Polish trackways have been read three different ways. Whether the earliest footprints were made on land, or only beside it, is an open question. Where researchers disagree, the episode says so.
It stays gentle throughout: no hunting, no peril, and it ends, deliberately, at the water's edge. The egg, and the first fully land-living animals, belong to a later evening.

title: Snowball Earth, When Ice Reached the Equator
description: Tonight is about a winter that lasted tens of millions of years. By the strongest reading of the evidence, twice, for millions of years at a stretch, ice reached the equator and a great deal of the ocean lay under it. And as far as anyone can currently show, nothing with a nervous system was alive to notice. The cast is microbes, algae, stone and ice, and the slow weather of a very long time.

It is told through what the stone kept: stones dropped into fine mud by melting ice, magnetism in old rock that puts glaciers near the equator, and a pale carbonate rock laid over the ice's debris on many continents. It is also, quietly, a story about the thaw, and about a warm sea afterwards.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. Whether the ocean was ever sealed from pole to pole is still argued between careful people, and the episode gives both sides their best case. What set the first freeze off is a leading idea, not a settled answer. How fast the thaw came, how long the pale rock took to form, and whether anything like an animal was already here are all open. Where researchers disagree, it says so.
It stays gentle throughout: nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and it ends on the far side of the ice.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the ice melts, that's the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: Whale Evolution, When Whales Still Walked
description: Tonight is about a family of animals that changed its way of life, over roughly ten million years, from living beside rivers to swimming in the open sea. It begins on the shore of an old, warm sea in what is now Pakistan and India.

It is told through what the bones and rocks kept: one small bone in the ear, a mother and her young preserved together in Pakistani stone, a four-legged traveller in Peru, and a valley in the Egyptian desert where about five hundred skeletons lie in what was once the floor of a sea.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. "Whale" is a loose word here, and "walked" describes only the first half of the story. Whether the animal named for walking could walk well, or at all, is disputed. Most ages are ranges. How the whales reached the Americas is a favoured hypothesis, and which hoofed animal is their nearest living relative is still argued. Where researchers disagree, it says so.
It stays gentle throughout: nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and it ends in a valley of sand that was once a warm sea.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the valley, that's the intended use.

title: The Ediacaran Period, Life Before the Cambrian
description: Tonight is about the long stretch of time before the Cambrian, about ninety-six million years of it, and about the first large bodies that left a mark in the rock. It begins at a pale band of limestone in a creek bed in South Australia, and it ends at a single trail in Newfoundland.

It is told through places: a deep, dark sea floor at Mistaken Point, where fronds were kept under volcanic ash; a quarry in Leicestershire, where a schoolgirl and then three schoolboys found a fossil in rock that was thought too old to hold one; a flat, ribbed oval called Dickinsonia; a trail the width of a grain of rice at Nilpena; and a few small white funnels in Namibia, among the first animals to build hard parts.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. Whether the branching fronds were animals is not known. Whether Dickinsonia was an animal rests on a chemical argument that others have questioned. What made some small round holes in the first shells, whether the Namibian reefs grew where they lie, how far the cold spell reached, and why the large bodies thin out near the end are all argued over. Where researchers disagree, it says so.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and the end of the period is told only as a before and an after, in the rock.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the trail, that's the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: The Mediterranean Salt Crisis, When the Door Closed
description: Tonight is about a sea and its door. About six million years ago the Mediterranean was cut off, or nearly cut off, from the Atlantic, and the rocks under its floor keep what followed: gypsum around its edges, a layer of salt a kilometre or more thick in its deep basins, and then, a little over five million years ago, the return of the Atlantic. It begins at the Strait of Gibraltar as it is today, and it ends at the same strait.

It is told through places and rock: a drilling ship in the early nineteen seventies; a filament no longer than two millimetres, lying in a crystal of gypsum in Piedmont; a last stage that may have been a lake or a sea; a channel under the strait, two hundred kilometres long; a low white cliff in Sicily where one kind of rock stops and another begins; and caves in the Italian hills.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. How far the water fell, whether about fifteen hundred metres or about six hundred, whether the deep basins ever dried, how long the salt took to form, what closed and opened the door, whether the last stage was a lake or a sea, and how fast the sea came back are all argued over. The famous version, that the Mediterranean dried up and was quickly refilled, is only one picture, and the episode says so.

It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, no one stands on a shore, and the refilling is told only through what the rock keeps: a groove, a field of smooth ridges, a line in a cliff.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the cliff in Sicily, that's the intended use.
Best with the lights off.

title: The Great Oxidation Event, The Rusting of the Sea
description: Tonight is about air, a sea, and the colour of some very old rock. About two and a half billion years ago the air held almost none of the oxygen that most living things now depend on, and many seas held a great deal of dissolved iron. Over the following half billion years the air changed, and the rock kept the record: stripes of iron on an old sea floor, red sandstone laid down on an old land, a black stone from a lake in Karelia, and a dark shale from Gabon. It begins in the air before the change and closes on the stripes the sea left behind.

It is told through places and rock rather than through creatures, because there is almost nothing living to show: a sulphur signal in ancient sediment, a hillside of ice-scratched stone in Ontario, a field of manganese in the Kalahari, a lake in the north of Russia, and the shales of Gabon.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. When the change began (the papers put it anywhere from about 2.5 to about 2.43 billion years ago), how fast it went, whether it was one event or a long rise and fall, how early the oxygen-makers were at work, whether ice reached the equator, whether the long high in the carbon record was global, whether the structures in Gabon are early multicellular life, and what ended the iron stripes are all argued over. The popular story that oxygen poisoned most life on Earth is told near the end as a story, with what could and could not be found.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and no one is harmed in the telling.
You do not need to follow any of it closely. If you're asleep before the black rock at Lake Onega, that's the intended use.

title: The Ice Ages, What the Ice Left Behind
description: Tonight is about ice, and about what ice leaves behind. Not the ice itself, which is gone from nearly every place it once lay, but the traces: a hillside in Sicily with a dark layer in it, a core of mud from the bottom of the sea, a bubble of very old air, a boulder on a prairie, a shoreline on a mountainside above a salt flat, a cliff of wind-blown dust, and a single line in a column of Greenland ice. It runs from about two and a half million years ago to about eleven thousand seven hundred years ago, the formal start of the epoch we live in now, and it ends on a look back across the whole of it.

It is told through places and traces rather than through creatures. The large animals of the ice age are not in it, and neither is anyone who lived then. The cast is stone, mud, ice, air, water and the smallest traces of plants.

A good deal of tonight is honestly unsettled. What started the great ice in the north, whether the orbit of the Earth is the pacemaker of the ice or only a nudge, why the beat of the ice changed about a million years ago, how low the sea fell, what the word "ice age" should mean, and even a counting slip of 99 years against 69 at the base of the present epoch are all argued over, or differ between the pages. Where the sources disagree the episode says so aloud and keeps the voices apart.
It stays gentle throughout. Nothing hunts, nothing is in peril, and no one is harmed in the telling.
